content: Breast diseases can be categorized as either disorders of the integumentary system or disorders of the reproductive system. Cancer The majority of breast diseases are noncancerous in nature. Breast Pain Breast pain is a common symptom associated with various breast conditions. Infections and Inflammations Infections and inflammations of the breast may arise due to trauma, milk stasis or engorgement, hormonal stimulation, infections, or autoimmune reactions. If these conditions occur repeatedly and are unrelated to lactation, an endocrinological evaluation is recommended. Pre-Malignant Diseases Carcinoma in situ is a pre-malignant condition that has the potential to progress into malignant breast cancer. Malignant Diseases Malignant breast diseases include breast cancer and Paget’s disease of the nipple, which is also referred to as Paget’s disease of the breast. Benign Conditions Benign breast conditions encompass a variety of disorders: Congenital Disorders: These include inverted nipples, supernumerary nipples, supernumerary breasts (also known as polymazia or polymastia), and duplicated nipples. Aberrations of Normal Development and Involution: These include cyclical nodularity, breast cysts, fibroadenomas (benign tumors), gynecomastia in males, nipple discharge (such as galactorrhea), and mammary fistulas. Fibrocystic Disease or Fibrocystic Changes: This condition includes the presence of cysts, epithelial hyperplasia, epithelial metaplasia, papillomas, and adenosis. Pregnancy-Related Conditions: These include galactocoeles, which are milk-filled cysts that can develop during or after pregnancy. Fibrocystic Breast Condition This condition is also referred to as fibrocystic breast disease, chronic cystic mastitis, diffuse cystic mastopathy, or mammary dysplasia. Nipple Discharge Abnormal discharge from the nipples can be a symptom of various underlying breast conditions. Abnormal Nipples Abnormalities of the nipples include inverted nipples, which may be congenital or acquired. Mastitis Mastitis refers to inflammation of the breast tissue and can occur due to various causes: Bacterial Mastitis: This is often associated with breastfeeding and milk stasis. Mastitis from Milk Engorgement or Secretory Stasis: This occurs when milk is not adequately drained from the breast. Mastitis of Mumps: This is a rare complication of mumps infection. Chronic Intramammary Abscess: This involves a persistent collection of pus within the breast tissue. Chronic Subareolar Abscess: This is a recurring abscess located beneath the areola. Tuberculosis of the Breast: This is a rare manifestation of tuberculosis infection in the breast. Syphilis of the Breast: This is an uncommon presentation of syphilis involving the breast tissue. Retromammary Abscess: This is an abscess located behind the breast tissue. Actinomycosis of the Breast: This is a rare bacterial infection caused by Actinomyces species. Mondor’s Disease: This is a rare condition involving thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast. Duct Ectasia Syndrome: This condition involves dilation and inflammation of the milk ducts, often leading to nipple discharge. Breast Engorgement: This occurs when the breasts become overly full of milk, leading to pain and swelling.
